questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following is always true about a spontaneous cell reaction in a galvanic cell?
questions.solution:
For a spontaneous cell reaction, the change in Gibbs free energy must be negative, i.e., $\Delta G \lt 0$.

The relationship between $\Delta G$, the standard Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^o$, and the reaction quotient $Q_C$ is given by:
$\Delta G = \Delta G^o + RT \ln Q_C$

At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q_C = K_C$, so:
$\Delta G^o = -RT \ln K_C$

Substituting this back into the first equation, we get:
$\Delta G = -RT \ln K_C + RT \ln Q_C = RT \ln \left( \dfrac{Q_C}{K_C} \right)$

For the reaction to be spontaneous ($\Delta G \lt 0$), we must have:
$RT \ln \left( \dfrac{Q_C}{K_C} \right) \lt 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{Q_C}{K_C} \lt 1 \Rightarrow Q_C \lt K_C$

In a standard galvanic cell, the standard cell potential is positive, $E^o_{cell} \gt 0$.
Since $\Delta G^o = -nFE^o_{cell}$, a positive $E^o_{cell}$ implies that $\Delta G^o \lt 0$.

Therefore, the correct conditions are $E^o_{cell} \gt 0$, $\Delta G^o \lt 0$, and $Q_C \lt K_C$.

Answer: $E^o_{cell} \gt 0;\ \Delta G^o \lt 0;\ Q_C \lt K_C$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The $\Delta$G$^o$ for the reaction, $\text{Cd}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Zn}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Cd}(s)$ is:
$\left[E^o_{\text{Cd}^{2+}/\text{Cd}} = -0.403,\ E^o_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.763\ V\right]$
questions.solution:
For the reaction $\text{Cd}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Zn}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Cd}(s)$, Zn is oxidized (anode) and $\text{Cd}^{2+}$ is reduced (cathode).

$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}}$

$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -0.403 - (-0.763) = 0.360\text{ V}$

The number of electrons transferred in the reaction is $n = 2$.

The standard Gibbs free energy change is given by:

$\Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}$

$\Delta G^{\circ} = -2 \times 96500 \times 0.360$

$\Delta G^{\circ} = -69480\text{ J} = -69.48\text{ kJ}$

Rounding to one decimal place, $\Delta G^{\circ} \approx -69.5\text{ kJ}$.

Answer: $-69.5\ kJ$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Resistance of 0.2 M solution of an electrolyte is 50 $\Omega$. The conductivity of the solution is 1.3 Sm$^{-1}$. If the resistance of 0.4 M solution of the same electrolyte is 260 $\Omega$, its molar conductivity is:
questions.solution:
The cell constant $G^*$ is given by the product of conductivity and resistance of the first solution:

$G^* = \kappa_1 \times R_1$

$G^* = 1.3\ S\ m^{-1} \times 50\ \Omega = 65\ m^{-1}$

The conductivity of the $0.4\ M$ solution, $\kappa_2$, is:

$\kappa_2 = \dfrac{G^*}{R_2} = \dfrac{65\ m^{-1}}{260\ \Omega} = 0.25\ S\ m^{-1}$

The concentration of the second solution in SI units is:

$C_2 = 0.4\ mol\ L^{-1} = 0.4 \times 10^3\ mol\ m^{-3} = 400\ mol\ m^{-3}$

The molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ is given by:

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa_2}{C_2}$

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{0.25\ S\ m^{-1}}{400\ mol\ m^{-3}} = 6.25 \times 10^{-4}\ S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}$

Answer: $6.25 \times 10^{-4}\ Sm^2mol^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Using the data given below, the strongest reducing agent is:
$E^o_{\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}/\text{Cr}^{3+}} = 1.33$ V $E^o_{\text{MnO}_4^-/\text{Mn}^{2+}} = 1.51$ V
$E^o_{\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^-} = 1.36$ V $E^o_{\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}} = -0.74$ V
questions.solution:
A reducing agent undergoes oxidation. The strength of a reducing agent is directly proportional to its standard oxidation potential, which is the negative of its standard reduction potential.

The standard oxidation potentials for the given species are:
$E^o_{\text{Cr}/\text{Cr}^{3+}} = -(-0.74) = +0.74$ V
$E^o_{\text{Cl}^-/\text{Cl}_2} = -1.36$ V
$E^o_{\text{Mn}^{2+}/\text{MnO}_4^-} = -1.51$ V
$E^o_{\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}} = -1.33$ V

Since $Cr$ has the highest standard oxidation potential ($+0.74$ V), it has the greatest tendency to get oxidized. Therefore, $Cr$ is the strongest reducing agent among the given options.

Answer: $Cr$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The quantity of Ca that can be produced from molten CaCl_2$, with the same quantity of electricity (in coulombs) required to produce 4.8 g of Mg from molten MgCl_2$ is:
[Atomic mass of Mg=24 u; Atomic mass of Ca=40 u]
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's second law of electrolysis, when the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes, the masses of the substances deposited are proportional to their equivalent weights.

$\dfrac{W_{Ca}}{W_{Mg}} = \dfrac{E_{Ca}}{E_{Mg}}$

Equivalent weight of Mg, $E_{Mg} = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$

Equivalent weight of Ca, $E_{Ca} = \dfrac{40}{2} = 20$

Given $W_{Mg} = 4.8$ g.

$\dfrac{W_{Ca}}{4.8} = \dfrac{20}{12}$

$W_{Ca} = \dfrac{20}{12} \times 4.8 = 8.0$ g

Answer: $8.0$ g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $3.482 \times 10^{-1}$g of Fe gets deposited when an aqueous solution of Ferric sulphate is electrolysed for 20 minutes using a current of "x" amperes. Find "x". (Atomic mass of Fe = 56amu).
questions.solution:
The chemical formula of ferric sulphate is $\text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$. The reduction reaction at the cathode is:

$\text{Fe}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}$

The number of electrons involved in the reduction of one $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ion is $3$. Thus, the equivalent mass of iron is $E = \dfrac{56}{3}$.

According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis:

$W = \dfrac{E \cdot I \cdot t}{96500}$

Given:
Mass deposited, $W = 3.482 \times 10^{-1} \text{ g} = 0.3482 \text{ g}$
Time, $t = 20 \text{ minutes} = 20 \times 60 = 1200 \text{ s}$
Current, $I = x$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$0.3482 = \dfrac{56 \cdot x \cdot 1200}{3 \cdot 96500}$

$0.3482 = \dfrac{67200 \cdot x}{289500}$

$x = \dfrac{0.3482 \cdot 289500}{67200}$

$x = \dfrac{100803.9}{67200} = 1.5 \text{ A}$

Answer: $1.5\text{A}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Consider a Galvanic cell in which the following reactions occurs: $\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Ag}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{Ag}(s)$. What is the standard potential of the cell? Given: $E^0_{(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag})} = aV$, $E^0_{(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe})} = bV$ & $E^0_{(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe})} = cV$
questions.solution:
The given cell reaction is $\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Ag}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{Ag}(s)$.

The standard cell potential is given by:
$E^0_{\text{cell}} = E^0_{\text{cathode}} - E^0_{\text{anode}} = E^0_{\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}} - E^0_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}}$

We are given:
$E^0_{\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}} = a$
$E^0_{\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}} = b$
$E^0_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}} = c$

To find $E^0_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}}$, we use the relation $\Delta G^0 = -nFE^0$.
For the half-reaction $\text{Fe}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}$, $\Delta G^0_1 = -3Fc$
For the half-reaction $\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}$, $\Delta G^0_2 = -2Fb$

The desired half-reaction is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first:
$\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$

The standard free energy change for this reaction is:
$\Delta G^0_3 = \Delta G^0_1 - \Delta G^0_2$
$-1 \times F \times E^0_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = -3Fc - (-2Fb)$
$-F E^0_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = -3Fc + 2Fb$
$E^0_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = 3c - 2b$

Substituting this back into the equation for the standard cell potential:
$E^0_{\text{cell}} = a - (3c - 2b)$
$E^0_{\text{cell}} = a + 2b - 3c$

Answer: $(a + 2b - 3c)\,V$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What will be the change in the electrode potential of chromium electrode dipping into chromic sulphate solution, when the electrolyte is diluted 10 times at $25^\circ$C? [ $E^0\ (\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr})] = -0.74$V
questions.solution:
The reduction half-reaction for the chromium electrode is:

$\text{Cr}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Cr}$

The Nernst equation for the reduction potential is given by:

$E = E^0 - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log \dfrac{1}{[\text{Cr}^{3+}]}$

$E = E^0 + \dfrac{0.0591}{3} \log [\text{Cr}^{3+}]$

Let the initial concentration of $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ be $c$. The initial electrode potential is:

$E_1 = E^0 + \dfrac{0.0591}{3} \log c$

When the solution is diluted 10 times, the new concentration becomes $\dfrac{c}{10}$. The new electrode potential is:

$E_2 = E^0 + \dfrac{0.0591}{3} \log \left(\dfrac{c}{10}\right)$

The change in electrode potential is:

$\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = \dfrac{0.0591}{3} \left[ \log \left(\dfrac{c}{10}\right) - \log c \right]$

$\Delta E = \dfrac{0.0591}{3} \log \left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)$

$\Delta E = \dfrac{0.0591}{3} \times (-1) = -0.0197 \text{ V}$

$\Delta E = -19.7 \text{ mV}$

The negative sign indicates that the electrode potential decreases by $19.7 \text{ mV}$.

Answer: Decrease by 19.7 mV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify the correct mathematical expression which represents the variation in molar conductivity of a weak acid having concentration C and ionisation constant $K_a$
($\lambda_m^\infty$ = molar conductivity at infinite dilution, $\lambda_m$ = molar conductivity at concentration C)
questions.solution:
The degree of dissociation $\alpha$ for a weak electrolyte is given by:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_m^\infty}$

For a weak acid, the ionisation constant $K_a$ is given by Ostwald's dilution law:

$K_a = \dfrac{C \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$

Substituting the expression for $\alpha$ into the equation for $K_a$:

$K_a = \dfrac{C \left( \dfrac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_m^\infty} \right)^2}{1 - \dfrac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_m^\infty}}$

$K_a = \dfrac{C \dfrac{\lambda_m^2}{(\lambda_m^\infty)^2}}{\dfrac{\lambda_m^\infty - \lambda_m}{\lambda_m^\infty}}$

$K_a = \dfrac{C \lambda_m^2}{\lambda_m^\infty (\lambda_m^\infty - \lambda_m)}$

Answer: $K_a = \lambda_m^2 C / \lambda_m^\infty(\lambda_m^\infty - \lambda_m)$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, one Assertion and the other Reason are given. Choose the right option.
Assertion: The Molar conductivity of KCl increases very slowly with dilution and approaches a limiting value when dilution is infinite.
Reason: In case of KCl there is an increase in the number of ions on dilution due to complete ionisation at infinite dilution.
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct
questions.solution:
KCl is a strong electrolyte and is completely ionised in solution at all concentrations. Therefore, the number of ions does not increase upon dilution.

The molar conductivity of a strong electrolyte like KCl increases slowly with dilution and approaches a limiting value at infinite dilution ($\Lambda_m^{\circ}$). This increase is not due to an increase in the number of ions, but rather due to a decrease in interionic attractions, which increases the mobility of the ions.

Thus, the Assertion is correct, but the Reason is incorrect.

Answer: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A current of 0.10 A was passed for 2 hours through a dilute solution of sulphuric acid. The total volume of gaseous products produced at STP is:
[Given: $1 \mathrm{~F}=96500 \mathrm{C}$; Molar volume at STP is $22.7 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ]
questions.solution:
The electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid involves the electrolysis of water. The reactions at the electrodes are as follows:

At cathode: $4H^{+}(aq) + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}(g)$

At anode: $2H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow O_{2}(g) + 4H^{+}(aq) + 4e^{-}$

The total charge passed $Q$ is given by $Q = I \times t = 0.10 \text{ A} \times (2 \times 3600 \text{ s}) = 720 \text{ C}$.

The number of moles of electrons passed is $n_{e} = \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{720}{96500} \approx 0.00746 \text{ mol}$.

From the stoichiometry, $4$ moles of electrons produce $2$ moles of $H_{2}$ and $1$ mole of $O_{2}$, totaling $3$ moles of gas. Thus, $4$ moles of electrons produce $3$ moles of gas.

Total moles of gas produced $n_{total} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times n_{e} = 0.75 \times 0.00746 = 0.005595 \text{ mol}$.

The volume of gas at STP is $V = n_{total} \times 22.7 \text{ L/mol} = 0.005595 \times 22.7 \approx 0.1270 \text{ L}$.

Converting to mL, $V = 0.1270 \times 1000 = 127 \text{ mL}$.

Answer: 127 mL

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify the two statements which are incorrect regarding Corrosion of Iron.
A. During electrical protection of underground Iron pipes from corrosion the connected Mg plate undergoes reduction.
B. At the Cathodic area on Iron the reaction occurring is $4 \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{O}_2+4 \mathrm{e} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$
C. Rust formed $\mathrm{Fe}_2 \mathrm{O}_3 . \mathrm{xH}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is an acidic oxide.
D. The $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions are obtained from water containing dissolved gases like $\mathrm{SO}_2, \mathrm{NO}_2$ or $\mathrm{CO}_2$.
questions.solution:
In the process of cathodic protection of iron pipes, a more reactive metal like magnesium is used as a sacrificial anode. The magnesium undergoes oxidation ($Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^{-}$) to protect the iron. Therefore, statement A is incorrect because Mg undergoes oxidation, not reduction.

At the cathodic area of iron corrosion, oxygen is reduced in the presence of moisture. The reaction is $O_2 + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_2O$. This is a standard cathodic reaction in acidic or neutral media, making statement B correct.

Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 \cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$. Iron(III) oxide is a basic oxide, not an acidic oxide. Therefore, statement C is incorrect.

The presence of dissolved acidic gases like $\mathrm{SO}_2$, $\mathrm{NO}_2$, or $\mathrm{CO}_2$ in water increases the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ ions, which accelerates the corrosion process. Thus, statement D is correct.

Since statements A and C are incorrect, the correct option is A & C.

Answer: A & C

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the cell
$\mathrm{Pt}\left|\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{~g})(1 \mathrm{bar})\right| \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \| \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \mid \mathrm{Cu}$

At 298 K , the emf of the cell is 0.31 V . The pH of the acidic solution is 3 . The concentration of $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ is:
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $\mathrm{H}_2(g) + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}^{+}(aq) + \mathrm{Cu}(s)$.

The standard cell potential $E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_2} = 0.34 \mathrm{V} - 0.00 \mathrm{V} = 0.34 \mathrm{V}$.

Using the Nernst equation at 298 K:

$E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$

Here $n = 2$, $Q = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]^2}{P_{\mathrm{H}_2} [\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$. Given $\mathrm{pH} = 3$, so $[\mathrm{H}^{+}] = 10^{-3} \mathrm{M}$. $P_{\mathrm{H}_2} = 1 \mathrm{bar}$.

$0.31 = 0.34 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \left( \dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{1 \times [\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} \right)$

$-0.03 = -0.02955 \log \left( \dfrac{10^{-6}}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} \right)$

Approximating $0.0591/2 \approx 0.03$, we get $1 \approx \log \left( \dfrac{10^{-6}}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} \right)$.

Therefore, $10^1 = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$, which implies $[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}] = 10^{-7} \mathrm{M}$.

Answer: $10^{-7} \mathrm{M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
In the reaction,
$F e_{(a q)}^{2+}+A g_{(a q)}^{+} \rightarrow F e_{(a q)}^{3+}+A g_{(s)}$

The standard emf $\left(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}\right)$ of the cell is:
$\left[\right.$ Given: $\left.E_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+} / \mathrm{Ag}}^o=a V ; \quad E_{\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} / \mathrm{Fe}}^o=b V ; E_{\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} / \mathrm{Fe}}^o=c V\right]$
questions.solution:
Oxidation (Anode): $Fe^{2+} \to Fe^{3+} + e^-$
Reduction (Cathode): $Ag^+ + e^- \to Ag$

$E°_{cell} = E°_{cathode} - E°_{anode} = E°_{Ag^+/Ag} - E°_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$

Finding $E°_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$ using Gibbs free energy:

Reaction 1: $Fe^{2+} + 2e^- \to Fe$, $E°_1 = b$, $\Delta G°_1 = -2Fb$
Reaction 2: $Fe^{3+} + 3e^- \to Fe$, $E°_2 = c$, $\Delta G°_2 = -3Fc$

Target (Reaction 2 $-$ Reaction 1): $Fe^{3+} + e^- \to Fe^{2+}$

$\Delta G°_3 = \Delta G°_2 - \Delta G°_1 = -3Fc - (-2Fb) = -3Fc + 2Fb$

$-1 \cdot F \cdot E°_3 = -3Fc + 2Fb \Rightarrow E°_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = 3c - 2b$

$E°_{cell} = a - (3c - 2b) = a + 2b - 3c$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The variation of the molar conductivity with concentration of an electrolyte $(X)$ in aqueous solution is shown in the given figure.
The electrolyte ' X ' is:
questions.solution:
The graph shows the variation of molar conductivity ($\lambda_m$) with the square root of concentration ($\sqrt{c}$).

For strong electrolytes like $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{KCl}$, and $\text{HNO}_3$, the molar conductivity increases linearly with decreasing concentration according to the Kohlrausch equation: $\lambda_m = \lambda_m^0 - A\sqrt{c}$. These electrolytes show a gradual increase in $\lambda_m$ as concentration decreases, and they can be extrapolated to infinite dilution to find $\lambda_m^0$.

For weak electrolytes like $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, the molar conductivity increases sharply as the concentration decreases, especially at very low concentrations. This is due to the increase in the degree of dissociation of the weak electrolyte as the solution is diluted. The curve for a weak electrolyte does not show a linear relationship with $\sqrt{c}$ and cannot be extrapolated to infinite dilution to determine $\lambda_m^0$.

The provided graph exhibits a sharp increase in $\lambda_m$ as $\sqrt{c}$ approaches zero, which is characteristic of a weak electrolyte. Among the given options, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is the only weak electrolyte.

Answer: $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
What is the standard electrode potential at 298 K for the reaction: $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+1 \mathrm{e}-\rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{+1}$ ?
Given: $\mathrm{E}_0 \mathrm{Cu}^{+1} / \mathrm{Cu}=0.5 \mathrm{~V} \quad \& \quad \mathrm{E}_0 \mathrm{Cu}^{+2} / \mathrm{Cu}=0.335 \mathrm{~V}$
questions.solution:
The standard electrode potential for the reaction $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{+}$ can be determined using the Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}$.

For the reaction $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$, $\Delta G^{\circ}_{1} = -2 \times F \times 0.335 = -0.67F$.

For the reaction $\mathrm{Cu}^{+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$, $\Delta G^{\circ}_{2} = -1 \times F \times 0.5 = -0.5F$.

The target reaction is $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{+}$, which is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first:

$\Delta G^{\circ}_{3} = \Delta G^{\circ}_{1} - \Delta G^{\circ}_{2} = -0.67F - (-0.5F) = -0.17F$.

Since $\Delta G^{\circ}_{3} = -nFE^{\circ}_{3}$ with $n=1$, we have $-1 \times F \times E^{\circ}_{3} = -0.17F$.

Therefore, $E^{\circ}_{3} = 0.17 \text{ V}$.

Answer: 0.17 V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $2 \text{Cr} + 3 \text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2 \text{Cr}^{3+} + 3 \text{Fe}$.

The standard cell potential $E^{0}_{cell}$ is calculated as $E^{0}_{cathode} - E^{0}_{anode}$.

$E^{0}_{cell} = E^{0}_{\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}} - E^{0}_{\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}} = -0.42 - (-0.72) = 0.30 \text{ V}$.

The number of electrons transferred in the balanced reaction is $n = 6$.

Using the Nernst equation at $298 \text{ K}$:

$E_{cell} = E^{0}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Cr}^{3+}]^2}{[\text{Fe}^{2+}]^3}$

$E_{cell} = 0.30 - \dfrac{0.0591}{6} \log \dfrac{(0.2)^2}{(0.02)^3}$

$E_{cell} = 0.30 - 0.00985 \log \dfrac{0.04}{0.000008}$

$E_{cell} = 0.30 - 0.00985 \log (5000)$

Since $\log(5000) = \log(5 \times 10^3) = \log(5) + 3 \approx 0.699 + 3 = 3.699$.

$E_{cell} = 0.30 - 0.00985 \times 3.699 \approx 0.30 - 0.0364 = 0.2636 \text{ V}$.

Answer: 0.2636 V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, one Assertion and the other Reason are given. Choose the correct option.
Assertion: For strong electrolytes the plot of Molar conductivity versus Concentration gives a straight line with slope equal to +A and intercept equal to $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$.
Reason: For strong electrolytes, $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ increases slowly with dilution due to increase in the distance between the ions and increase in ionic mobility
options: Both Assertion and Reason are incorrect.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct.
questions.solution:
The molar conductivity $\lambda_{m}$ of a strong electrolyte varies with concentration $C$ according to the Kohlrausch equation: $\lambda_{m} = \lambda_{m}^{\circ} - A\sqrt{C}$, where $\lambda_{m}^{\circ}$ is the molar conductivity at infinite dilution and $A$ is a constant.

The plot of $\lambda_{m}$ versus $\sqrt{C}$ is a straight line with a negative slope equal to $-A$ and an intercept equal to $\lambda_{m}^{\circ}$. The Assertion states the slope is $+A$ and the intercept is $\lambda_{m}$, which is incorrect.

For strong electrolytes, $\lambda_{m}$ increases slowly with dilution because the inter-ionic attractions decrease as the distance between the ions increases, leading to an increase in ionic mobility. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Answer: Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A current of 1.5 A is passed for 2 hours through an aqueous solution of $\mathrm{Pd} \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{n}}$ where X is a monovalent anion. During the electrolysis process 2.977 g of Palladium metal gets deposited at the cathode. Calculate the charge on Pd ions. (Atomic mass of Pd $=106.4 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ ).
questions.solution:
The total charge $Q$ passed through the solution is given by $Q = I \times t$.

Given $I = 1.5$ A and $t = 2$ hours $= 2 \times 3600$ s $= 7200$ s.

$Q = 1.5 \times 7200 = 10800$ C.

The number of moles of electrons passed is $n_e = \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{10800}{96500} \approx 0.1119$ mol.

The mass of Palladium deposited is $m = 2.977$ g and the atomic mass is $M = 106.4$ g/mol.

The number of moles of Palladium deposited is $n_{Pd} = \dfrac{m}{M} = \dfrac{2.977}{106.4} \approx 0.02798$ mol.

The reaction at the cathode is $\mathrm{Pd}^{n+} + n e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Pd}$.

The stoichiometric ratio is $n = \dfrac{n_e}{n_{Pd}} = \dfrac{0.1119}{0.02798} \approx 4$.

Therefore, the charge on the Palladium ion is $n = 4$.

Answer: $\mathrm{n}=4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The Standard Reduction potential at 25°C for $(\text{MnO}_4)^{-1}/\text{H}^+$ is +1.49 V. The $E^0$ values for four redox couples:
(a). $\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}$,  (b). $\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}$,  (c). $\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}$ and  (d). $\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}$ are +1.81 V, –0.74 V, +1.50 V and +0.8 V respectively.
Identify the two reduced species which cannot be oxidised by $(\text{MnO}_4)^{-1}/\text{H}^+$
questions.solution:
$(MnO_4)^-/H^+$ has $E° = +1.49$ V. It can only oxidise species whose $E°$ is less than $+1.49$ V.

Species with $E° \gt $ +1.49 V cannot be oxidised by permanganate:

$Co^{3+}/Co^{2+}$: $E° = +1.81$ V > +1.49 V ⇒ cannot be oxidised

$Au^{3+}/Au$: $E° = +1.50$ V > +1.49 V ⇒ cannot be oxidised

$Cr^{3+}/Cr$: $E° = -0.74$ V < +1.49 V ⇒ can be oxidised

$Ag^+/Ag$: $E° = +0.8$ V < +1.49 V ⇒ can be oxidised

The two species that cannot be oxidised are (a) and (c).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify the two incorrect electrochemical reactions shown as taking place in the given cells at the respective electrodes.
CellElectrodeReaction
Lead-Storage CellCathode$Pb + 2SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+ + 2e^- \to PbSO_4 + 2H_2O + SO_2$
Leclanche CellCathode$MnO_2 + NH_4^+ + 2e^- \to MnO + OH + NH_3$
Mercury CellAnode$Zn/Hg + 2OH^- \to ZnO(s) + H_2O + 2e^-$
Fuel CellCathode$O_2(g) + 2H_2O + 4e^- \to 4OH^-$
questions.solution:
In a lead-storage cell, the cathode reaction involves the reduction of lead dioxide to lead sulfate: $\mathrm{PbO}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-} + 4\mathrm{H}^+ + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{PbSO}_4 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$. The reaction given in the table for the lead-storage cell cathode is incorrect as it shows $\mathrm{Pb}$ instead of $\mathrm{PbO}_2$ and includes $\mathrm{SO}_2$.

In a Leclanche cell, the cathode reaction involves the reduction of manganese dioxide: $2\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{NH}_4^+ + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_3 + 2\mathrm{NH}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$. The reaction given in the table is incorrect as it shows $\mathrm{MnO}$ and $\mathrm{OH}$ instead of the standard products.

In a mercury cell, the anode reaction is $\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + 2\mathrm{OH}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 2\mathrm{e}^-$, which is correctly represented in the table.

In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, the cathode reaction is $\mathrm{O}_2(g) + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 4\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 4\mathrm{OH}^-$, which is correctly represented in the table.

Therefore, the reactions for the lead-storage cell (A) and the Leclanche cell (B) are incorrect.

Answer: A & B

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When $0.1 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ of KCl was filled in a Conductivity cell the resistance was 80 ohms at 298 K . (Conductivity of 0.1 M KCl at 298 K is $1.29 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$. The same cell when filled with an unknown electrolyte of concentration 0.025 M , had a resistance of 92 ohms. What is the Molar conductivity of the electrolyte at the given concentration?
questions.solution:
The cell constant $G^{*}$ is given by the product of conductivity $\kappa$ and resistance $R$. For the KCl solution, $\kappa_{KCl} = 1.29 \text{ S m}^{-1} = 1.29 \times 10^{-2} \text{ S cm}^{-1}$.

$G^{*} = \kappa_{KCl} \times R_{KCl} = 1.29 \times 10^{-2} \text{ S cm}^{-1} \times 80 \Omega = 1.032 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

For the unknown electrolyte, the conductivity $\kappa_{unk}$ is calculated using the cell constant and the measured resistance $R_{unk} = 92 \Omega$.

$\kappa_{unk} = \dfrac{G^{*}}{R_{unk}} = \dfrac{1.032 \text{ cm}^{-1}}{92 \Omega} \approx 0.011217 \text{ S cm}^{-1}$.

The molar conductivity $\Lambda_{m}$ is defined as $\Lambda_{m} = \dfrac{1000 \times \kappa}{C}$, where $C$ is the concentration in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Given $C = 0.025 \text{ M}$, we have:

$\Lambda_{m} = \dfrac{1000 \times 0.011217}{0.025} = \dfrac{11.217}{0.025} = 448.68 \text{ S cm}^{2} \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Rounding to the nearest provided option, the value is $448.7 \text{ S cm}^{2} \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $448.7 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a cell $2 \mathrm{M}_{(\mathrm{S})}+\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g})+4 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{M}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{l})}$ the $\mathrm{E}^0$ cell $=+1.67 \mathrm{~V}$. When $\left[\mathrm{M}^{2+}\right]$ is $1.0 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{M}$ and $\mathrm{p}\left(\mathrm{O}_2\right)$ is 0.1 atm , the EMF of the cell becomes +1.57 V . Calculate the pH of the electrochemical cell.
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $2M_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} + 4H^+_{(aq)} \rightarrow 2M^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}$.

The Nernst equation for the cell is $E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$, where $n=4$ electrons are transferred.

The reaction quotient $Q$ is given by $Q = \dfrac{[M^{2+}]^2}{p(O_2) [H^+]^4}$.

Substituting the given values: $1.57 = 1.67 - \dfrac{0.0591}{4} \log \left( \dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{0.1 \times [H^+]^4} \right)$.

$-0.10 = -\dfrac{0.0591}{4} \log \left( \dfrac{10^{-6}}{0.1 \times [H^+]^4} \right)$.

$\dfrac{0.10 \times 4}{0.0591} = \log \left( \dfrac{10^{-5}}{[H^+]^4} \right)$.

$6.768 = \log(10^{-5}) - \log([H^+]^4) = -5 - 4 \log[H^+]$.

Since $pH = -\log[H^+]$, we have $6.768 = -5 + 4(pH)$.

$4(pH) = 11.768$.

$pH = \dfrac{11.768}{4} = 2.942$.

Rounding to the nearest option, the pH is approximately $2.94$.

Answer: $2.94$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For the cell reaction $4 \mathrm{Br}^{-}+\mathrm{O}_2+4 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Br}_2+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ at 298 K , the $\mathrm{E}^0$ cell $=0.16 \mathrm{~V}$.
What would be the $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}$ (Equilibrium constant) value if the reverse reaction were to take place?
questions.solution:
For the reverse reaction, $E°_{rev} = -0.16$ V and $n = 4$.

Using $E° = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K_c$:

$-0.16 = \dfrac{0.059}{4}\log K_c$

$\log K_c = \dfrac{-0.16 \times 4}{0.059} = \dfrac{-0.64}{0.059} \approx -10.847$

$K_c = 10^{-10.847} \approx 1.422 \times 10^{-11}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, one Assertion and the other Reason, are given. Choose the correct option.
Assertion: During the electrolysis of aqueous $\mathrm{NaCl}, \mathrm{Cl}_2$ is liberated at the anode in preference to $\mathrm{O}_2$ and water gets reduced to $\mathrm{H}_2$ at cathode.
Reason: The reaction at Anode with lower oxidation potential is not preferred due to over potential of Oxygen.
options: Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct.
Both Assertion and Reason are incorrect.
questions.solution:
In the electrolysis of aqueous $\mathrm{NaCl}$, the competing reactions at the anode are:

1. $2\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl}_2(g) + 2e^{-}$, $E^{\circ} = 1.36 \mathrm{V}$

2. $2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(l) \rightarrow \mathrm{O}_2(g) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(aq) + 4e^{-}$, $E^{\circ} = 1.23 \mathrm{V}$

Although the standard oxidation potential for water is lower, the evolution of oxygen gas at the anode requires an additional overpotential. Due to this overpotential, the oxidation of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ occurs preferentially, leading to the liberation of $\mathrm{Cl}_2$ gas. At the cathode, the reduction of water ($2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 + 2\mathrm{OH}^{-}$) is preferred over the reduction of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ because the reduction potential of water ($-0.83 \mathrm{V}$) is higher than that of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ ($-2.71 \mathrm{V}$). Thus, the Assertion is correct.

The Reason states that the reaction at the anode with lower oxidation potential is not preferred due to the overpotential of oxygen. This is a correct explanation for why the reaction with a higher standard potential (chloride oxidation) occurs instead of the reaction with a lower standard potential (water oxidation). Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The EMF of the cell $\mathrm{Al} / \mathrm{Al}^{3+}(0.01 \mathrm{M}) \| \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(0.02 \mathrm{M}) / \mathrm{Fe}$ is 1.209 V . The EMF of the cell can be increased by ------------------------------
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $2\mathrm{Al}(s) + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Al}^{3+}(aq) + 3\mathrm{Fe}(s)$.

The Nernst equation for the cell EMF is given by $E_{cell} = E^{0}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$, where $Q = \dfrac{[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]^3}$ and $n = 6$.

Substituting the expression for $Q$: $E_{cell} = E^{0}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{6} \log \left( \dfrac{[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]^3} \right)$.

To increase $E_{cell}$, the value of the term $\log \left( \dfrac{[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]^3} \right)$ must be decreased. This can be achieved by either decreasing the numerator $[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]$ or increasing the denominator $[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]$.

Among the given options, increasing the concentration of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ will decrease the value of $Q$, thereby increasing the EMF of the cell.

Answer: increasing the concentration of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The conductivity of 0.01 M solution of $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$ at 298 K is $1.65 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{Scm}^{-1}$
What is the $\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{a}}$ value of the acid if $\lambda^0\left(\mathrm{H}^{+}\right)$and $\lambda^0\left(\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COO}\right)^{-1}$ are $349.1 \mathrm{Scm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and $40.9 \mathrm{Scm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively?
questions.solution:
The molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ is given by the formula $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}$, where $\kappa = 1.65 \times 10^{-4} \text{ S cm}^{-1}$ and $C = 0.01 \text{ M}$.

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{1.65 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{0.01} = 16.5 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

The limiting molar conductivity $\Lambda_m^0$ is $\lambda^0(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^0(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-) = 349.1 + 40.9 = 390.0 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

The degree of dissociation $\alpha$ is given by $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^0} = \dfrac{16.5}{390.0} \approx 0.0423$.

The dissociation constant $K_a$ is given by $K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$. Since $\alpha$ is small, $1 - \alpha \approx 1$.

$K_a \approx C\alpha^2 = 0.01 \times (0.0423)^2 = 0.01 \times 0.001789 = 1.789 \times 10^{-5}$.

The $\text{pK}_a$ value is $-\log_{10}(K_a) = -\log_{10}(1.789 \times 10^{-5}) = 5 - \log_{10}(1.789) \approx 5 - 0.2526 = 4.747$.

Answer: $4.75$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
What is the reduction potential of a half-cell consisting of a Pt electrode dipped in $2.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ and $0.04 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ solution where the reaction taking place is conversion of $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions to $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ?
$\mathrm{E}^0\left(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} / \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\right)=0.771 \mathrm{~V}$
questions.solution:
The reduction half-reaction is given by $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$.

Using the Nernst equation for the electrode potential at $298 \mathrm{K}$:

$E = E^{0} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log \dfrac{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}]}$

Given $E^{0} = 0.771 \mathrm{V}$, $n = 1$, $[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}] = 2.2 \mathrm{M}$, and $[\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}] = 0.04 \mathrm{M}$.

Substituting the values:

$E = 0.771 - \dfrac{0.0591}{1} \log \left( \dfrac{2.2}{0.04} \right)$

$E = 0.771 - 0.0591 \log(55)$

Since $\log(55) \approx 1.74036$:

$E = 0.771 - 0.0591 \times 1.74036$

$E = 0.771 - 0.10285$

$E \approx 0.66815 \mathrm{V}$

Answer: 0.668 V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A current of 2.5 amperes is passed through 800 ml of 0.48 M solution of $\mathrm{CuSO}_4$ for 1.0 hour with a current efficiency of $80 \%$. If the volume of the solution remains unchanged, what is the final molarity of the solution?
questions.solution:
The reaction at the cathode is $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}(s)$.

The total charge passed through the solution is $Q = I \times t \times \text{efficiency} = 2.5 \text{ A} \times (1.0 \times 3600 \text{ s}) \times 0.80 = 7200 \text{ C}$.

The number of moles of electrons transferred is $n_{e} = \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{7200}{96500} \approx 0.07461 \text{ mol}$.

Since 2 moles of electrons are required to reduce 1 mole of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions, the moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ consumed is $n_{\text{Cu}^{2+}} = \dfrac{n_{e}}{2} = \dfrac{0.07461}{2} = 0.037305 \text{ mol}$.

The initial moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in 800 ml (0.8 L) of 0.48 M solution is $n_{\text{initial}} = 0.48 \text{ M} \times 0.8 \text{ L} = 0.384 \text{ mol}$.

The final moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ remaining is $n_{\text{final}} = 0.384 - 0.037305 = 0.346695 \text{ mol}$.

The final molarity is $M_{\text{final}} = \dfrac{n_{\text{final}}}{V} = \dfrac{0.346695}{0.8} \approx 0.43336 \text{ M}$.

Answer: $0.433$

$\mathrm{Cu}(s)+\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}(0.01 \mathrm{M}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(0.1 \mathrm{M})+\mathrm{Sn}(s)$
The gibbs free energy change for above mention reaction at NTP is $x \times 10^{-1} \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$. The value of $x$ is $\qquad$ [Nearest integer]
$\left[\right.$ Given $E_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}}^{\circ}=0.34 \mathrm{~V}, E_{\mathrm{Sn}^{2+} / / \mathrm{sn}}^{\circ}=-0.14 \mathrm{~V}F=96500 \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{mol}]$
questions.solution:
Given,
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \mathrm{Cu}(s)+\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}(0.01 \mathrm{M}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(0.1 \mathrm{M})+\mathrm{Sn}(s) \\ \\ & E_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}=E_{\text {cathode }}^{\circ}-E_{\text {anoode }}^{\circ} \\ \\ & =-0.14-(0.34)=-0.48 \mathrm{~V} \\ \\ & E_{\text {cell }}=E_{\text {cell }}^*-\frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{\left[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}\right]}[n=2] \\ \\ & =-0.48-\frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{[0.1]}{0.01} \\ \\ & =-0.48-0.0290 \log [10]=-0.5095 \mathrm{~V} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
$\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$ undergoes disproportionation, according to the equation,
$
2 \mathrm{Cu}^{+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+\mathrm{Cu}
$
The $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}$ value for the reaction is:
$[\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}}^{\mathrm{o}}=0.34 \mathrm{~V} \text { and } \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}^{+}}^{\mathrm{O}}=0.15 \mathrm{~V}]$
questions.solution:
The given disproportionation reaction is $2 \mathrm{Cu}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + \mathrm{Cu}$.

This reaction can be split into two half-reactions:
1) Oxidation: $\mathrm{Cu}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + e^{-}$ (where $E^{\circ}_{ox} = -E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}^{+}} = -0.15 \text{ V}$)
2) Reduction: $\mathrm{Cu}^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$ (where $E^{\circ}_{red} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{+}/\mathrm{Cu}}$)

To find $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{+}/\mathrm{Cu}}$, we use the Gibbs free energy relation $\Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}$.
For $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$, $\Delta G^{\circ}_{1} = -2 \times F \times 0.34 = -0.68F$.
For $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{+}$, $\Delta G^{\circ}_{2} = -1 \times F \times 0.15 = -0.15F$.
Subtracting the second from the first gives $\mathrm{Cu}^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$, with $\Delta G^{\circ}_{3} = \Delta G^{\circ}_{1} - \Delta G^{\circ}_{2} = -0.68F - (-0.15F) = -0.53F$.
Thus, $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = -\Delta G^{\circ}_{3} / (1 \times F) = 0.53 \text{ V}$.

The standard cell potential for the disproportionation reaction is $E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{ox} + E^{\circ}_{red} = -0.15 \text{ V} + 0.53 \text{ V} = +0.38 \text{ V}$.

Answer: $+0.38$ V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The limiting molar conductivity of $\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{OH}$ is $238 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. At $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, molar conductance of $0.1 \mathrm{M}$ aqueous solution of ammonium hydroxide is $9.54 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. The degree of ionisation of $\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{OH}$ at the same concentration and temperature is:
questions.solution:
The degree of ionisation $\alpha$ of a weak electrolyte is given by the ratio of the molar conductivity at a given concentration $\Lambda_m^c$ to the limiting molar conductivity $\Lambda_m^{\circ}$.

$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m^c}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}}$

Given values are $\Lambda_m^c = 9.54 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 238 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$\alpha = \dfrac{9.54}{238} \approx 0.040084$

To express this as a percentage, multiply by 100:

$\alpha \% = 0.040084 \times 100 = 4.0084 \%$

Answer: 4.008%

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}$ values of $\mathrm{A} . \mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{C}$ are given. Which element/(s) is/(are) good for coating the surface of iron to prevent corrosion?
Given: $[\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} / \mathrm{Fe}}^0=-0.44 \mathrm{~V} ; \quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{A}^{2+} / \mathrm{A}}^0=-2.37 \mathrm{~V} ; \quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}^{2+} / \mathrm{B}}^0=-0.15 \mathrm{~V} ; \quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}^{2+} / \mathrm{C}}^0=+0.34 \mathrm{~V}]$
questions.solution:
To prevent the corrosion of iron, the metal used for coating must act as a sacrificial anode. This means the coating metal must have a more negative standard reduction potential than that of iron ($E^{\circ}_{Fe^{2+}/Fe} = -0.44 \text{ V}$).

Comparing the given standard reduction potentials:
$E^{\circ}_{A^{2+}/A} = -2.37 \text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{B^{2+}/B} = -0.15 \text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{C^{2+}/C} = +0.34 \text{ V}$

Since $-2.37 \text{ V} \lt -0.44 \text{ V}$, element A has a lower reduction potential than iron. Therefore, element A can act as a sacrificial anode and protect iron from corrosion.

Elements B and C have reduction potentials greater than $-0.44 \text{ V}$, meaning they are more noble than iron and would not provide sacrificial protection.

Answer: Element A only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the incorrect statement among the following.
options: Electrolytic conductance increases with increase in temperature
Conductivity does not depend on the viscosity of the solution
Conductivity depends on the size of the ions
Conductivity depends on the solvation of the ions
questions.solution:
(1) Correct: With increase in temperature, kinetic energy of ions increases and viscosity of solvent decreases → ions move faster → conductance increases.

(3) Correct: Larger ions move more slowly → lower mobility → lower conductivity.

(4) Correct: Greater solvation → larger effective ionic radius → lower mobility → lower conductivity.

(2) Incorrect: Ion mobility is inversely proportional to viscosity of the solution. Higher viscosity → greater resistance to ion movement → lower conductivity. So conductivity does depend on viscosity.

Incorrect statement: (2)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When 0.1 mole of $\mathrm{MnO}_4{ }^{2-}$ is oxidised, the quantity of electricity required to completely oxidise $\mathrm{MnO}_4{ }^{2-}$ to $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}$ is
questions.solution:
The oxidation reaction of manganate ion to permanganate ion is given by:

$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} + e^{-}$

In this reaction, the oxidation state of manganese changes from $+6$ to $+7$. Thus, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{2-}$ requires $1$ mole of electrons for complete oxidation to $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$.

Given that $0.1$ mole of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{2-}$ is to be oxidized, the number of moles of electrons required is $0.1$ mole.

The quantity of electricity $Q$ is given by $Q = n \times F$, where $n$ is the number of moles of electrons and $F$ is the Faraday constant ($96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$).

$Q = 0.1 \text{ mol} \times 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1} = 9650 \text{ C}$.

Answer: 9650 C

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A dry cell consists of a moist paste of $\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{Cl}$ and $\mathrm{ZnCl}_2$ contained in a $\mathrm{Zn}$ casing which encloses a Carbon rod surrounded by black $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ paste. What is the role of $\mathrm{ZnCl}_2$ in it?
options: It acts as the anode while Carbon rod acts as the cathode.
It prevents pressure being developed in the cell due to $\mathrm{NH}_3$ gas formation.
It serves as cathode thus permitting Carbon rod to act as anode.
It keeps the contents dry and prevents leakage of electrolyte.
questions.solution:
In a Leclanche dry cell, the zinc casing acts as the anode and the carbon rod acts as the cathode. The electrolyte is a moist paste of $\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}$ and $\mathrm{ZnCl}_2$.

The chemical reaction at the cathode involves the reduction of $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ and the production of ammonia gas, $\mathrm{NH}_3$. Specifically, $\mathrm{NH}_4^{+}$ ions react to form $\mathrm{NH}_3$.

The $\mathrm{NH}_3$ gas produced would otherwise build up pressure inside the cell. $\mathrm{ZnCl}_2$ reacts with $\mathrm{NH}_3$ to form a complex salt, $[\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{NH}_3)_2\mathrm{Cl}_2]$, which prevents the accumulation of ammonia gas and the resulting pressure buildup.

Answer: It prevents pressure being developed in the cell due to $\mathrm{NH}_3$ gas formation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Arrange the following redox couples in the increasing order of their reducing strength:
$\begin{array}{ll}
{[\mathrm{A}]=\mathrm{Cu} / \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}} & \mathrm{E}^0=-0.34 \mathrm{~V} \\
{[\mathrm{~B}]=\mathrm{Ag} / \mathrm{Ag}^{+}} & \mathrm{E}^0=-0.8 \mathrm{~V} \\
{[\mathrm{C}]=\mathrm{Ca} / \mathrm{Ca}^{2+}} & \mathrm{E}^0=+2.87 \mathrm{~V} \\
{[\mathrm{D}]=\mathrm{Cr} / \mathrm{Cr}^{3+}} & \mathrm{E}^0=+0.74 \mathrm{~V}
\end{array}$
questions.solution:
The reducing strength of a species is determined by its standard oxidation potential. A higher standard oxidation potential ($E^{0}_{ox}$) indicates a stronger reducing agent. The given values are standard oxidation potentials ($E^{0}_{ox}$) for the couples $M/M^{n+}$.

The values are:
A: $Cu/Cu^{2+}$, $E^{0}_{ox} = -0.34$ V
B: $Ag/Ag^{+}$, $E^{0}_{ox} = -0.8$ V
C: $Ca/Ca^{2+}$, $E^{0}_{ox} = +2.87$ V
D: $Cr/Cr^{3+}$, $E^{0}_{ox} = +0.74$ V

Comparing the values:
$-0.8 \lt -0.34 \lt +0.74 \lt +2.87$

This corresponds to the order:
B < A < D < C

Thus, the increasing order of reducing strength is B < A < D < C.

Answer: B < A < D < C

questions.q: What is the quantity of charge, in Faraday units, required for the reduction of 3.5 moles of $\mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O} 7^{2-}$ in acid medium?
questions.solution:
The reduction half-reaction for the dichromate ion in an acidic medium is given by:

$\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-} + 14\mathrm{H}^{+} + 6\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} + 7\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

From the balanced equation, it is observed that 1 mole of $\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}$ requires 6 moles of electrons for its reduction.

Since 1 mole of electrons corresponds to 1 Faraday of charge, 1 mole of $\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}$ requires 6 Faraday of charge.

For 3.5 moles of $\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}$, the total charge required is:

Charge = $3.5 \text{ moles} \times 6 \text{ Faraday/mole} = 21.0 \text{ Faraday}$

Answer: 21.0

questions.q:
Given below are 2 statements: Assertion and Reason. Choose the correct option.
Assertion: When Molar conductivity for a strong electrolyte is plotted versus $\sqrt{C}(\mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L})^{1 / 2}$, a straight line is obtained with intercept equal to Molar conductivity at infinite dilution for the electrolyte and Slope equal to $-\mathrm{A}$. All electrolytes of a given type have the same $\mathrm{A}$ value.
Reason: At infinite dilution, strong electrolytes of the same type will have different number of ions due to incomplete dissociation.
options: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect statement.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct statement.
Both Assertion and Reason are incorrect statements.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
questions.solution:
The molar conductivity of a strong electrolyte varies with concentration according to the Kohlrausch equation: $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\circ} - A\sqrt{C}$. This equation represents a straight line when $\Lambda_m$ is plotted against $\sqrt{C}$, where the intercept is $\Lambda_m^{\circ}$ (molar conductivity at infinite dilution) and the slope is $-A$. The constant $A$ depends on the type of electrolyte (e.g., 1:1, 1:2, 2:1) and the solvent properties, meaning all electrolytes of a given type in a given solvent have the same $A$ value. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

The Reason states that at infinite dilution, strong electrolytes of the same type have a different number of ions due to incomplete dissociation. This is incorrect because strong electrolytes are considered to be completely dissociated at all concentrations, including at infinite dilution. Furthermore, the number of ions produced per formula unit is determined by the stoichiometry of the electrolyte, which is constant for a given type of electrolyte. Therefore, the Reason is an incorrect statement.

Answer: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect statement.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A current of 3.0A is passed through 750 ml of 0.45 M solution of CuSO_4$ for 2 hours with a current efficiency of 90%. If the volume of the solution is assumed to remain constant, what would be the final molarity of CuSO_4$ solution?
questions.solution:
The reaction for the electrolysis of CuS$O_{4}$ is Cu$^{2+}$ + 2e$^{-} \rightarrow$ Cu(s). \\ \\ The total charge passed through the solution is $Q = I \times t \times \text{efficiency}$. \\ \\ $Q = 3.0 \text{ A} \times (2 \times 3600 \text{ s}) \times 0.90 = 19440 \text{ C}$. \\ \\ The number of moles of electrons passed is $n_{e} = \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{19440}{96500} \approx 0.20145 \text{ mol}$. \\ \\ Since 2 moles of electrons are required to reduce 1 mole of Cu$^{2+}$, the moles of Cu$^{2+}$ reduced is $n_{\text{reduced}} = \dfrac{n_{e}}{2} = \dfrac{0.20145}{2} = 0.100725 \text{ mol}$. \\ \\ The initial moles of CuSO_{4}$ is $n_{\text{initial}} = M \times V = 0.45 \text{ M} \times 0.750 \text{ L} = 0.3375 \text{ mol}$.

The final moles of CuSO_{4}$ is $n_{\text{final}} = n_{\text{initial}} - n_{\text{reduced}} = 0.3375 - 0.100725 = 0.236775 \text{ mol}$. \\ \\ The final molarity is $M_{\text{final}} = \dfrac{n_{\text{final}}}{V} = \dfrac{0.236775}{0.750} = 0.3157 \text{ M} \approx 0.316 \text{ M}$.

Answer: 0.316

questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $\mathrm{Cd}(s) + 2\mathrm{H}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cd}^{2+}(aq) + \mathrm{H}_{2}(g)$.

The standard cell potential $E^{0}_{cell}$ is calculated as $E^{0}_{cathode} - E^{0}_{anode}$.

Given $E^{0}(\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_{2}) = 0.00 \text{ V}$ and $E^{0}(\mathrm{Cd}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cd}) = -0.40 \text{ V}$.

$E^{0}_{cell} = 0.00 - (-0.40) = 0.40 \text{ V}$.

Using the Nernst equation at $298 \text{ K}$:

$E_{cell} = E^{0}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log \dfrac{[\mathrm{Cd}^{2+}] P_{\mathrm{H}_{2}}}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]^{2}}$

Here $n = 2$, $[\mathrm{Cd}^{2+}] = 0.01 \text{ M}$, $[\mathrm{H}^{+}] = 0.02 \text{ M}$, and $P_{\mathrm{H}_{2}} = 0.8 \text{ atm}$.

$E_{cell} = 0.40 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \dfrac{0.01 \times 0.8}{(0.02)^{2}}$

$E_{cell} = 0.40 - 0.02955 \log \dfrac{0.008}{0.0004}$

$E_{cell} = 0.40 - 0.02955 \log(20)$

Since $\log(20) = \log(2 \times 10) = 0.3010 + 1 = 1.3010$.

$E_{cell} = 0.40 - 0.02955 \times 1.3010$

$E_{cell} = 0.40 - 0.03844 = 0.36156 \text{ V} \approx 0.3616 \text{ V}$.

Answer: 0.3616 V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $0.1 \mathrm{M}$ solution of $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ is taken in a Conductivity cell and a potential difference of $40 \mathrm{~V}$ is applied across the ends of a column of this solution whose diameter is $4.0 \mathrm{~cm}$ and length of the column is $12 \mathrm{~cm}$. The current used is $0.4 \mathrm{~A}$. The Molar conductivity of the solution is _________.
questions.solution:
The resistance $R$ of the solution is given by Ohm's law: $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{40 \text{ V}}{0.4 \text{ A}} = 100 \Omega$.

The area of cross-section $A$ of the column is $\pi r^2$. Given diameter $d = 4.0 \text{ cm}$, the radius $r = 2.0 \text{ cm}$. Thus, $A = \pi \times (2.0 \text{ cm})^2 = 4\pi \text{ cm}^2 \approx 12.566 \text{ cm}^2$.

The cell constant $G^{*}$ is given by $\dfrac{l}{A}$, where $l = 12 \text{ cm}$. So, $G^{*} = \dfrac{12}{4\pi} = \dfrac{3}{\pi} \text{ cm}^{-1} \approx 0.9549 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

The conductivity $\kappa$ is given by $\kappa = \dfrac{G^{*}}{R} = \dfrac{3/\pi}{100} = \dfrac{3}{100\pi} \text{ S cm}^{-1} \approx 0.009549 \text{ S cm}^{-1}$.

The molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ is calculated using the formula $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{1000 \times \kappa}{C}$, where $C = 0.1 \text{ M}$.

Substituting the values: $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{1000 \times (3 / (100\pi))}{0.1} = \dfrac{30}{\pi \times 0.1} = \dfrac{300}{\pi} \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Calculating the value: $\Lambda_m \approx \dfrac{300}{3.14159} \approx 95.493 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Rounding to the nearest option, we get $95.5 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $95.5 \mathrm{~Scm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

$\begin{aligned}
& \left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{N a B r}-\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{N a C l}=\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{KCl}}-\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{KBr}} \\
& \left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{HCl}}+\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{KOH}}-\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{KCl}}=\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}} \\
& \left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{KBr}}-\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{NaBr}}=\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{NaBr}}-\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{Nal}} \\
& \left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{N H_4 \mathrm{Cl}}-\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{NO}_3}=\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{N H_4 \mathrm{Cl}}-\left(\Lambda_m^0\right)_{N H 4 B r}
\end{aligned}$
questions.solution:
Using Kohlrausch's law, expanding Equation 2 LHS: $(A^0_m)_{HCl} + (A^0_m)_{KOH} - (A^0_m)_{KCl}$

$= [\lambda^0(H^+) + \lambda^0(Cl^-)] + [\lambda^0(K^+) + \lambda^0(OH^-)] - [\lambda^0(K^+) + \lambda^0(Cl^-)]$

$= \lambda^0(H^+) + \lambda^0(OH^-)$

$= (A^0_m)_{H_2O}$ = RHS

Equation 2 is correct. The cancellation of $\lambda^0(Cl^-)$ and $\lambda^0(K^+)$ on both sides confirms LHS = RHS.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Propane in presence of $\mathrm{O}_2$ gas undergoes complete combustion to produce $\mathrm{CO}_2$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$. The required $\mathrm{O}_2$ for this combustion reaction was produced by the electrolysis of water. For what duration of time had water been electrolysed by passing $200 \mathrm{~A}$ current so that Oxygen gas produced could completely burn $44 \mathrm{~g}$ of Propane?
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of propane is:
$\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8} + 5\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_{2} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The molar mass of propane ($\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8}$) is $3 \times 12 + 8 \times 1 = 44 \text{ g/mol}$.

Moles of propane = $\dfrac{44 \text{ g}}{44 \text{ g/mol}} = 1 \text{ mol}$.

From the stoichiometry, $1 \text{ mol}$ of propane requires $5 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_{2}$.

The electrolysis of water is given by:
$2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$

For $1 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_{2}$ produced, $4 \text{ moles}$ of electrons are required (since each oxygen atom changes oxidation state from $-2$ to $0$, and there are $2$ oxygen atoms per $\text{O}_{2}$ molecule).

Total moles of electrons required for $5 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_{2}$ = $5 \times 4 = 20 \text{ mol}$.

Using Faraday's law of electrolysis, $Q = n \times F = I \times t$, where $F \approx 96500 \text{ C/mol}$.

$20 \times 96500 = 200 \times t$

$t = \dfrac{20 \times 96500}{200} = 9650 \text{ seconds}$.

Converting to hours: $t = \dfrac{9650}{3600} \approx 2.68 \text{ hours}$.

Answer: 2.68 hours

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If electrolysis of water is carried out for a time duration of 2 hours, how much electric current in amperes would be required to liberate $100 \mathrm{~ml}$ of $\mathrm{O}_2$ gas measured under standard conditions of temperature and pressure?
questions.solution:
The electrolysis of water produces oxygen gas at the anode according to the reaction: $2H_2O(l) \rightarrow O_2(g) + 4H^{+}(aq) + 4e^{-}$.

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $4$ moles of electrons are required to produce $1$ mole of $O_2$ gas. At standard temperature and pressure (STP), $1$ mole of any gas occupies $22.4$ liters or $22400$ ml.

The volume of $O_2$ given is $100$ ml. The number of moles of $O_2$ produced is $n_{O_2} = \dfrac{100}{22400} = \dfrac{1}{224}$ moles.

The total charge $Q$ required is $n_{e^{-}} \times F$, where $n_{e^{-}} = 4 \times n_{O_2} = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{224} = \dfrac{1}{56}$ moles of electrons and $F = 96500$ C/mol.

$Q = \dfrac{96500}{56} \approx 1723.21$ Coulombs.

The time duration is $2$ hours, which is $2 \times 3600 = 7200$ seconds.

The current $I$ is given by $I = \dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{1723.21}{7200} \approx 0.2393$ A.

Answer: 0.2393 A

questions.q:
The reaction taking place in a galvanic cell is as given
$\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{B}^{2+}\left(\mathrm{1} \mathrm{1} \mathrm{1 0} \mathrm{0}^{-\mathrm{M}} \mathrm{M}\right) \rightarrow \mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})}+\mathrm{A}^{2+}(0.1 \mathrm{M}).$
The emf of the cell is $+2.651 \mathrm{~V}$. If the standard emf of the cell is $+2.71 \mathrm{~V}$, what is the value of $\mathrm{X}$ ?
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{B}^{2+}(10^{-X} \mathrm{M}) \rightarrow \mathrm{B}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{A}^{2+}(0.1 \mathrm{M})$.

The Nernst equation for the cell at $298 \mathrm{K}$ is given by $E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$, where $n$ is the number of electrons transferred.

Here, $n = 2$, $E_{\text{cell}} = 2.651 \mathrm{~V}$, and $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 2.71 \mathrm{~V}$.

The reaction quotient $Q$ is $\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{B}^{2+}]} = \dfrac{0.1}{10^{-X}} = 10^{X-1}$.

Substituting the values into the Nernst equation:

$2.651 = 2.71 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log(10^{X-1})$

$2.651 - 2.71 = -0.02955 \times (X-1)$

$-0.059 = -0.02955 \times (X-1)$

$X-1 = \dfrac{0.059}{0.02955} \approx 2$

$X = 2 + 1 = 3$.

Answer: X = 3

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When Lead Storage battery is in the process of getting charged which one of the following reactions takes place?
options: $\mathrm{SO}_3$ gas gets liberated and $\mathrm{PbO}_{2(\mathrm{~s})}$ is formed.
questions.solution:
In a lead storage battery, the discharge reaction is: $\mathrm{Pb}_{(s)} + \mathrm{PbO}_{2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO}_{4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{(l)}$.

During the charging process, the reaction is reversed by applying an external potential. The reaction becomes: $2\mathrm{PbSO}_{4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb}_{(s)} + \mathrm{PbO}_{2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4(aq)}$.

In this process, $\mathrm{PbSO}_{4(s)}$ at the cathode is reduced to $\mathrm{Pb}_{(s)}$, and $\mathrm{PbSO}_{4(s)}$ at the anode is oxidized to $\mathrm{PbO}_{2(s)}$.

Thus, $\mathrm{PbSO}_{4(s)}$ is converted into $\mathrm{Pb}_{(s)}$ and $\mathrm{PbO}_{2(s)}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{PbSO}_{4(\mathrm{~s})}$ gets converted to $\mathrm{Pb}_{(\mathrm{S})}$ and $\mathrm{PbO}_{2(\mathrm{~s})}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The Molar conductivity of $0.05 \mathrm{M}$ solution of $\mathrm{MgCl}_2$ is $194.5 \mathrm{~ohm}^{-1} \mathrm{~cm}^2$ per mole at room temperature. A Conductivity cell with electrodes having $3.0 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ surface area and $1.0 \mathrm{~cm}$ apart is filled with the solution of $\mathrm{MgCl}_2$. What would be the resistance offered by the conductivity cell?
questions.solution:
The molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ is related to the conductivity $\kappa$ and molarity $C$ by the formula $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{1000 \times \kappa}{C}$.

Given $\Lambda_m = 194.5 \text{ ohm}^{-1} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $C = 0.05 \text{ M}$, we calculate the conductivity $\kappa$ as follows:

$\kappa = \dfrac{\Lambda_m \times C}{1000} = \dfrac{194.5 \times 0.05}{1000} = \dfrac{9.725}{1000} = 0.009725 \text{ S cm}^{-1}$.

The cell constant $G^{*}$ is defined as $\dfrac{l}{A}$, where $l$ is the distance between electrodes and $A$ is the surface area of the electrodes.

$G^{*} = \dfrac{1.0 \text{ cm}}{3.0 \text{ cm}^2} = 0.3333 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

The relationship between conductivity $\kappa$, resistance $R$, and cell constant $G^{*}$ is $\kappa = \dfrac{G^{*}}{R}$.

Rearranging for resistance $R$:

$R = \dfrac{G^{*}}{\kappa} = \dfrac{0.3333}{0.009725} \approx 34.27 \text{ ohms}$.

Answer: 34.27 ohms

questions.q:
Match the items in Column I with their description in Column II

B$E_{cell}^0$QExtensive property.
CMolar conductivityRDecreases with decrease in concentration of both strong and weak electrolytes.
D$\Delta G_{cell}$SIncreases with dilution.
questions.solution:
Kappa (K) is the specific conductivity, which is defined as the conductance of a unit volume of solution. It decreases with a decrease in concentration (dilution) because the number of ions per unit volume decreases.

Standard cell potential ($\mathrm{E_{cell}^0}$) is an intensive property because it does not depend on the amount of substance in the system.

Molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) is defined as the conductivity of a solution containing one mole of electrolyte. It increases with dilution because the volume of the solution containing one mole of electrolyte increases, leading to greater dissociation (for weak electrolytes) and reduced inter-ionic attractions (for strong electrolytes).

Gibbs free energy change ($\mathrm{\Delta G_{cell}}$) is an extensive property because it depends on the amount of substance undergoing the reaction in the cell.

Matching the items:
A (Kappa) matches R (Decreases with decrease in concentration).
B ($\mathrm{E_{cell}^0}$) matches P (Intensive property).
C (Molar conductivity) matches S (Increases with dilution).
D ($\mathrm{\Delta G_{cell}}$) matches Q (Extensive property).

Thus, the correct mapping is A=R, B=P, C=S, D=Q.

Answer: $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{R} \quad \mathrm{B}=\mathrm{P} \quad \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{S} \quad \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{Q}$

Cathode: $2\text{H}^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}(g)$
Overall reaction: $\text{Fe}(s) + 2\text{H}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{H}_{2}(g)$

The standard cell potential $E^{\circ}_{cell}$ is calculated as:
$E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode}$
$E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0.00 \text{ V} - (-0.44 \text{ V}) = 0.44 \text{ V}$

Using the Nernst equation at $25^{\circ} \text{C}$:
$E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Fe}^{2+}] \cdot P_{\text{H}_{2}}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}$
Here $n = 2$, $[\text{Fe}^{2+}] = 0.001 \text{ M}$, $[\text{H}^{+}] = 0.01 \text{ M}$, and $P_{\text{H}_{2}} = 1 \text{ bar}$.

$E_{cell} = 0.44 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \dfrac{0.001 \times 1}{(0.01)^{2}}$
$E_{cell} = 0.44 - 0.02955 \log \dfrac{10^{-3}}{10^{-4}}$
$E_{cell} = 0.44 - 0.02955 \log(10)$
$E_{cell} = 0.44 - 0.02955 \approx 0.41 \text{ V}$

Answer: $0.41 \mathrm{~V}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the molar conductance of $0.025 \mathrm{M}$ aqueous solution of calcium chloride at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The specific conductance of calcium chloride is $12.04 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{Sm}^{-1}$
questions.solution:
The molar conductance $\Lambda_m$ is given by the formula $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{C}$, where $\kappa$ is the specific conductance and $C$ is the molar concentration.

Given:
$\kappa = 12.04 \times 10^{-2} \text{ S m}^{-1}$
$C = 0.025 \text{ M} = 0.025 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$

Convert concentration to $\text{mol m}^{-3}$:
$1 \text{ L} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$
$C = 0.025 \text{ mol} / 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3 = 25 \text{ mol m}^{-3}$

Substitute the values into the formula:
$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{12.04 \times 10^{-2} \text{ S m}^{-1}}{25 \text{ mol m}^{-3}}$
$\Lambda_m = 0.4816 \times 10^{-2} \text{ S m}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Express in scientific notation as required by the options:
$\Lambda_m = 481.6 \times 10^{-5} \text{ S m}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $481.6 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{Sm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Given that molar conductances for $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$, $\mathrm{BaCl}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{Cl}$ are $523.28,280.0$ and $129.8\Omega^{-1} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively. What is the molar conductivity $\left(\Omega^{-1} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$ of $\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{OH}$ ?
questions.solution:
According to Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions, the molar conductivity of an electrolyte at infinite dilution is the sum of the molar conductivities of its constituent ions.

The given molar conductivities are:
$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{OH}^{-}) = 523.28$
$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{BaCl}_{2}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}) = 280.0$
$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}) = 129.8$

We need to find $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{OH}^{-})$.

Using the given values, we can express $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH})$ as:
$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}) = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}) + \dfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}) - \dfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{BaCl}_{2})$

Substituting the values:
$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}) = 129.8 + \dfrac{523.28}{2} - \dfrac{280.0}{2}$
$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}) = 129.8 + 261.64 - 140.0$
$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}) = 391.44 - 140.0 = 251.44$

Answer: $251.44$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The specific conductivity of a solution containing $1.0 \mathrm{~g}$ of anhydrous $\mathrm{BaCl}_{2}$ in $200 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the solution has been found to be $0.0058 \mathrm{Scm}^{-1}$. The molar and equivalent conductivity of the solution respectively are
questions.solution:
The molar mass of $\mathrm{BaCl}_{2}$ is $137.3 + 2 \times 35.5 = 208.3 \mathrm{~g/mol}$.

The number of moles of $\mathrm{BaCl}_{2}$ is $n = \dfrac{1.0 \mathrm{~g}}{208.3 \mathrm{~g/mol}} \approx 0.0048008 \mathrm{~mol}$.

The molarity $M$ of the solution is $M = \dfrac{n}{V(\text{in L})} = \dfrac{0.0048008 \mathrm{~mol}}{0.200 \mathrm{~L}} = 0.024004 \mathrm{~M}$.

The molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ is calculated as $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{M} = \dfrac{0.0058 \mathrm{~S cm}^{-1} \times 1000 \mathrm{~cm}^3 \mathrm{L}^{-1}}{0.024004 \mathrm{~mol L}^{-1}} \approx 241.626 \mathrm{~S cm}^2 \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$.

For $\mathrm{BaCl}_{2}$, the n-factor is 2 (since $\mathrm{BaCl}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ba}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$).

The equivalent conductivity $\Lambda_{eq}$ is calculated as $\Lambda_{eq} = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{n\text{-factor}} = \dfrac{241.626}{2} \approx 120.813 \mathrm{~S cm}^2 \mathrm{eq}^{-1}$.

Rounding to the nearest values provided in the options, we get $241.6 \mathrm{~S cm}^2 \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ and $120.83 \mathrm{~S cm}^2 \mathrm{eq}^{-1}$.

Answer: $241.6 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and $120.83 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \mathrm{eq}^{-1}$
